A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARC-Encoder and retain matching methods and experiments. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and complete Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original context-compression and long-context experiments, decoder adaptation, architecture ablations, and computational and storage measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds biomedical evaluations, retrieval and context-length analyses, further pooling experiments, and smaller-model evaluations.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains query averaging, the linear bottleneck projector, frozen decoders, reconstruction/continuation pretraining, and decoder-specific adaptation. The additional pooling variants and smaller backbones are experimental configurations of this retained method.

E1.justification: v2 adds PubMedQA and BioASQ, extending evaluation to biomedical domains absent from the fine-tuning mixture. Appendix A.6 also introduces Needle-in-Haystack retrieval across context lengths and insertion depths, testing precise information recovery beyond the original task coverage. Original datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: The original comparator families remain: ICAE-like, xRAG-like, LLMLingua2, PISCO-like, open/closed-book models, and the existing long-context alternatives. Additional ICAE rows vary chunking and compression settings of the retained baseline; the new biomedical and retrieval evaluations reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: Added protocols include fixed-chunk ICAE comparisons at matched compression ratios, biomedical F1 evaluation, context-length bins, judge-scored retrieval across lengths/depths, and 1.1B/1.8B encoders paired with a 3B decoder. Reported settings also change: the memory-token ablation specifies 32 tokens in v1 Table 8 versus 16 in v2 Table 6, and Figure 5 relabels pretraining PF=32 as PF=64. These unexplained revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds pooling-placement controls, expands average-versus-last-query pooling to 4× compression, and introduces biomedical distribution-shift tests, context-length stratification, Needle-in-Haystack analysis, and smaller-model efficiency studies. These investigate several previously untested robustness and design questions. The HotpotQA/SQuAD specialization analysis already existed in v1 Appendix A.1.

E5.justification: v2 adds standard deviations to the architecture and pooling ablations in Tables 5–6. Their predecessors already reported averages over three fine-tuning seeds, so this adds uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs. The principal benchmark comparisons still report point estimates.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover biomedical QA, matched-ratio ICAE comparisons, pooling placement, retrieval, and smaller models. Existing shared-encoder scores also change under the retained Table 1 setting: with Mistral, NQ changes from 36.4 to 38.2 while HotpotQA changes from 43.6 to 40.8. The original long-context results in Table 3 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The FLOP assumptions and derivations in v1 Appendix B.1 are retained in v2 Appendix B, including equations (1)–(3). No new formal definitions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical corrections appear.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace state-of-the-art claims with claims of strong performance. v2 also makes generalization to new domains more explicit and clarifies compatibility with a predefined decoder set. The four central contributions remain substantially the same.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability boundaries. It links long-context summarization weaknesses to training-distribution mismatch, explains fixed-memory-token advantages on short translation inputs, and discusses pooling-placement robustness. The new limitations discussion identifies task-format dependence, high-compression degradation, and limited native context sizes; the broader-impact statement additionally explains that compressed representations do not ensure confidentiality.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit answer-normalization details and implementation information for new configurations, while retaining most training and evaluation appendices. It removes the Common Crawl quality-score cutoff and the release statement and links for training code, models, and fine-tuning data. This reduces documented access information without establishing that the resources themselves were withdrawn.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for Chevalier et al.'s context compression, vision-based compression, and Activation Beacon, plus sources for the biomedical and Needle-in-Haystack evaluations. These broaden the existing positioning without replacing its central relationship to encoder-based compression and frozen decoders.

P1.justification: v2 makes local explanatory and language revisions, promotes profiling into Section 4.5, adds an in-domain/out-of-domain section, and expands the conclusion to include limitations. The overall introduction–related work–method–experiments structure and most existing methodological prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different journal layout and substantially expands the displays with new comparison tables, context-length plots, retrieval heatmaps, and smaller-model profiling figures. Existing displays gain uncertainty annotations and a training-diagram legend. Profiling moves into the main text, the adaptation diagram moves to the appendix, and some appendix results are additionally displayed as main-text subsets.

improvement.justification: v2 better supports applicability and design claims through biomedical/retrieval tests, matched-compression controls, ablation uncertainty, and explicit limitations. However, it removes release links and introduces inconsistent ICAE averages in Table 13: 20.6 and 18.1 do not match the displayed score means of approximately 36.8 and 31.8. These access and reporting regressions temper the stronger evidence, leaving a qualified net improvement.
